analysis.one_liner: Bars prepayment penalties, balloon payments, and negative amortization on high-cost home loans.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill got a Senate Banking Committee hearing in May 1993, but in September its provisions were folded into a broader committee bill and S. 924 itself never came up for a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets high-cost mortgages — mainly second mortgages and home-equity loans that carry rates far above normal, fees over 8% of the loan, or borrowers whose debt payments would eat more than 60% of their income. It would require lenders to warn borrowers in plain language, three days before closing, that they could lose their home, and it would ban some of the harshest loan terms: prepayment penalties, balloon payments, negative amortization, and fees for refinancing with the same lender. It would also let borrowers recover all finance charges and fees from lenders who break the rules, let state attorneys general sue, and hold investors who buy these loans responsible too.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners taking out high-cost home-equity or second mortgages — often older homeowners and borrowers with damaged credit — who would get clearer warnings before risking their home and stronger legal recourse when lenders stack loans with fees and penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Defines a 'high cost mortgage' as a home-secured loan with a rate more than 10 percentage points above comparable Treasury yields, closing points and fees above 8% of the loan, or total monthly debt payments above 60% of gross income, and covers loans made through brokers or by anyone originating two or more such loans a year. [S2] [S3]

Requires written, plainly-worded disclosures at least three business days before closing — including a warning that the lender holds a mortgage on the borrower's home and the borrower could lose it — and bars lenders from changing loan terms after the disclosures are given. [S3]

Prohibits prepayment penalties (except one month's interest if the loan is paid off within 90 days), balloon payments, negative amortization where the balance grows, advance payments consolidated into the loan proceeds, and points or fees charged to refinance with the same lender or an affiliate. [S2] [S3]

Adds a civil remedy letting borrowers recover all finance charges and fees paid on a violating loan, allows state attorneys general to enforce the rules within five years, and makes purchasers of these loans (assignees) liable for claims the borrower could raise against the original lender. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and brokers making high-cost home-equity and second mortgages, who would lose fee and prepayment-penalty income and face liability for violations, and investors who buy those loans on the secondary market.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-cost mortgage lenders and loan buyers

drawbacks.text: Tighter rules and assignee liability could raise the cost of, or reduce access to, home-equity credit for borrowers with poor credit histories, who have fewer lenders willing to serve them. [S3]

The definitions could miss abusive loans priced just under the thresholds, since a loan only qualifies above the 10-point rate gap, 8% fee, or 60% debt-to-income lines, and the Federal Reserve could change the debt-to-income trigger. [S3]
The bill would not take effect until the Federal Reserve issued regulations, up to 180 days after enactment plus 60 days, delaying any protection. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the targeted borrowers, the protections are substantial: the loan types covered were notorious for stripping home equity through fees and penalties, and the bill attacks exactly those tools while giving real teeth through civil recovery, state enforcement, and assignee liability. The main cost is possibly tighter credit for weak-credit borrowers, and the thresholds leave room for loans engineered to fall just outside them — a serious but manageable design limit.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee held a hearing in May 1993, then in September ordered the bill's provisions folded into a broader committee bill instead of advancing S. 924 itself, and the Senate never voted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 7, 1993 by Senator Riegle with five cosponsors, three Democrats and two Republicans, and referred to the Banking Committee. [S1] [S4] [S5]
The committee held hearings on May 19, 1993. [S5]
On September 21, 1993, the committee ordered the bill's provisions incorporated into S. 1275 rather than reporting S. 924 itself; S. 924 never reached a Senate vote. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Borrowers eventually got a version of these protections when the vehicle bill (S. 1275) became law in 1994 carrying a modified Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act — well-documented history outside the provided record — but without some of this bill's strongest terms, such as assignee liability. As the provided record ends, high-cost home-equity lenders were better off: they had avoided the standalone bill's full restrictions through no recorded opposition of their own.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost home-equity lenders, under the record shown

industries.note: These lenders make money on rates far above market, fees over 8% of the loan, prepayment penalties, and repeated refinancing fees on second mortgages secured by borrowers' homes — the exact practices the bill bans and makes legally actionable. Ordinary borrowers' savings come directly out of this revenue.

industries.industry: Mortgage brokers in the high-cost loan market
industries.note: The bill treats anyone originating a high-cost loan through a broker, or originating two or more a year, as a 'creditor' subject to the disclosure and liability rules, closing a gap brokers could otherwise operate through.

Assignee liability would let borrowers pursue investors who bought these loans, cutting off the common practice of originating abusive loans and selling them, which shifts the risk away from the lender. This provision did not appear in the law as eventually enacted.
